item.title: Delhi's dense urban landscape extends along the banks of India's Yamuna River
item.summary: Acquired on 10 September 2026 by one of the Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites, this false-colour image shows built-up areas in purple and magenta tones ...
item.page_text:
Delhi, the metropolitan area which includes India’s capital, New Delhi, covers a vast and densely built expanse in the plains of northern India. The Yamuna River, a major tributary of the Ganges, winds through the city, flowing across housing, transport networks, commercial districts, green spaces, and agricultural land.
Acquired on 10 September 2026 by one of the Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellites, this false-colour image shows built-up areas in purple and magenta tones and vegetation in bright green. The dark waters of the Yamuna River run through the image from north to south-east, and the runways of the Indira Gandhi International Airport are visible in the south-west of the image.
Copernicus Sentinel satellite data support the monitoring of urban sprawl and land cover change, contributing to urban planning, green space protection, and sustainable environmental management.

item.title: Autumn Paints Poland’s Bieszczady Mountains
item.summary: Fall color covers the forested slopes of Bieszczady National Park, while patches of polonina, a type of high-mountain meadow, have turned tan.
item.page_text:
Fall color covers the forested slopes of Bieszczady National Park, while patches of polonina, a type of high-mountain meadow, have turned tan.
As the air grows cooler and days shorter, brown bears prowl the Carpathian Mountains of southern Poland with the goal of fattening up ahead of winter hibernation. In a more conspicuous sign of autumn, beech and other deciduous trees blanketing the hillsides start to sport reds and golds. The seasonal transformation was underway in southeast Poland’s Bieszczady National Park on October 8, 2026, when the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite captured this image.
European beech ( Fagus sylvatica ) dominates the area’s forests, with other species such as sycamore maple ( Acer pseudoplatanus ) also contributing to vibrant color in the fall. Dropping air temperatures and waning daylight cause these trees to curtail the production of chlorophyll , the molecule that plants use to synthesize food. Without it, the leaves’ green pigments fade, allowing the yellows and reds of other pigments to show through.
A descendent of ice-age survivors, the European beech has persisted across millennia in a range of climates. After the glaciers retreated, beech forests spread northward across the European continent from isolated refugia in the Carpathians, Alps, and other mountain ranges, and played a crucial role in reforesting the previously ice-covered land. Portions of Bieszczady National Park are included within UNESCO’s network of ancient and primeval beech forests spanning 18 countries.
Expansive as their footprint across Europe may be, beech forests reach only so high in elevation—about 1,000 to 1,260 meters (3,300 to 4,100 feet)—in this area. Above that is the realm of the polonina , a Slavic term for subalpine meadow, consisting of open grasslands and shrubby thickets of rowan (mountain ash), willows, and green alder. Patches of polonina stretch across ridge tops to the east-southeast of Smerek and appear tan, having lost their summer greenness .
The Bieszczady Mountains are renowned not only for forests and mountain meadows but also for charismatic wildlife. European bison, once extinct in the wild , were reintroduced to the area in the 1960s and now roam the hills by the hundreds, according to recent surveys . Additionally, populations of brown bears and Eurasian lynx find refuge and ample food sources in the forests.
NASA Earth Observatory image by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey . Story by Lindsey Doermann.

item.title: Sentinel-3C captures Hurricane Rachel
item.summary: Image: Demonstrating that the visible channels of Sentinel-3C’s sea and land surface temperature radiometer are working as expected, on 2 October the instrument captured this image of Hurricane Rachel over the eastern Pacific Ocean, off the coast of Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula.
item.page_text:
You have already liked this page, you can only like it once!
Demonstrating that the visible channels of Sentinel-3C’s sea and land surface temperature radiometer are working as expected, on 2 October the instrument captured this image of Hurricane Rachel over the eastern Pacific Ocean, off the coast of Mexico and the Baja California Peninsula. The image marks another important milestone in the commissioning of Europe’s newest Copernicus Sentinel-3 satellite, offering an early glimpse of the instrument’s capabilities as it is being prepared to deliver valuable observations of Earth’s surface.
Sentinel-3C, the third in the series of Copernicus Sentinel-3 satellites, was launched on 15 September. The European Space Agency is, therefore, still in the early stages of commissioning this new satellite for service.
Identical to its older siblings, Sentinel-3C carries a suite of instruments to systematically measure Earth’s oceans, land, cryosphere and atmosphere. The satellite’s ocean and land colour instrument and its synthetic aperture radar altimeter have already returned their first images . Now, as this image of Hurricane Rachel shows, its sea and land surface temperature radiometer is also offering a glimpse of what’s in store.
The instrument observes Earth across nine spectral bands spanning the visible, shortwave infrared and thermal infrared parts of the electromagnetic spectrum, as well as two dedicated channels for fire detection. Its primary role is to measure sea- and land-surface temperatures using thermal its thermal infrared channels.
The visible channels support this process by detecting clouds to prevent contamination of temperature measurements. They also support aerosol retrieval and atmospheric correction, contributing to the quality and accuracy of the instrument's data products. Since this is a false-colour image, vegetation on land appears red.
This image offers a first glimpse from the instrument’s visible channels only – images using its thermal channels are still to come – stay tuned.

item.page_text:
There are 89,603 registered dogs in New York City.
Dog owners are required to obtain a license for their pets, registering details including the dog's name, breed and birth year, along with the owner's ZIP code.
Every Dog in New York is an interactive map that puts this canine census on the map, revealing which breeds dominate individual neighborhoods, where particular dog names are most popular, and how the city's dog population has changed over time.
Using the map you can search for a breed, a dog's name, or a neighborhood to discover where your pooch would fit in - and where they would stand out from the crowd. The map is colored by the most common dog breed in each neighborhood.
Labrador Retrievers (including crossbreeds) lead in 75 of the 197 neighborhoods, followed by Yorkshire Terriers in 58 and Shih Tzus in 39. You can also explore the breeds that are most distinctive to particular areas: those that appear disproportionately often compared with their citywide popularity.
There are plenty of other ways to dig into the data. You can filter the map by borough, highlight neighborhoods with above-average numbers of dogs per home, or hide the quarter of neighborhoods with the fewest dogs. And if you fancy a little canine cartographic mischief, you can even sink Staten Island.
The map sidebar includes links to some intriguing trends in the city's dog population. For example the huge 25% jump in dogs born in 2020 and the end of New York's French Bulldog boom in 2016.

item.title: NASA's SpaceX launch lights up the sky with a giant glowing jellyfish | ScienceDaily
item.summary: Date: October 17, 2026; Source: NASA ; Summary: A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket created a dazzling, jellyfish-shaped glow across the eastern United States ...
item.page_text:
A SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket transformed the early morning sky into a spectacular display of light on October 13, 2026. As the rocket climbed above Earth carrying a Dragon spacecraft, sunlight illuminated its expanding exhaust plumes, creating an enormous glowing shape that resembled a jellyfish.
This striking phenomenon, known as a "jellyfish," occurs when a rocket launches near sunrise or sunset. Sunlight reaches the exhaust high in the atmosphere, making the spreading plume shine brightly against the darker sky below.
SpaceX Launch Creates a Spectacular Sky Display
The mission lifted off at 6:33 a.m. EDT from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. The illuminated exhaust plumes were visible across the eastern United States, giving observers a remarkable view of the rocket's journey into space.
The launch marked SpaceX's 35th commercial resupply mission for NASA, delivering scientific experiments, essential supplies, and equipment to the International Space Station.
New Space Station Upgrades and Medical Experiments
Among the cargo aboard Dragon is the final set of International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays, known as IROSAs. These additional solar panels are scheduled for installation later this fall and will help provide electricity for the orbiting laboratory.
The spacecraft is also transporting equipment for several scientific investigations that could lead to important advances in medicine and materials science.
One experiment will explore manufacturing artificial retinas in microgravity, where the near absence of gravity creates conditions that cannot easily be reproduced on Earth. The research could help develop technologies to restore vision in people with certain forms of vision loss.
Another investigation will use 3D heart tissue models to support the development of more efficient drug testing methods during future space missions.
Additional experiments will examine how a new type of glass forms in microgravity and investigate brain organoids, miniature models of brain tissue grown from cells. These models could help researchers identify new targets for treating neurological conditions, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and multiple sclerosis.

item.title: Hubble Space Telescope Spots Dusty Spiral Galaxy: NGC 1827 | Sci.News
item.summary: Astronomers using the NASA / ESA Hubble Space Telescope have captured a new view of NGC 1827, an intermediate spiral galaxy seen edge-on in the ...
item.page_text:
Astronomers using the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope have captured a new view of NGC 1827, an intermediate spiral galaxy seen edge-on in the constellation Columba.
This Hubble image shows the edge-on, intermediate spiral galaxy NGC 1827. Image credit: NASA / ESA / Michael Jones, California Institute of Technology / Gladys Kober, NASA / Catholic University of America.
NGC 1827 resides approximately 37 million light-years away from Earth in the southern constellation of Columba.
This galaxy was discovered by the British astronomer John Herschel on November 28, 1837.
Otherwise known as ESO 362-6, LEDA 16849 or IRAS 05083-3701, it belongs to the NGC 1792/1808 group of galaxies.
The new image of NGC 1827 was captured with Hubble’s Advanced Camera for Surveys (ACS) instrument.
“The image reveals bright-blue regions along the galaxy’s disk dotted with dark dust lanes where new stars are likely forming,” the Hubble astronomers said in a statement .
“A bright foreground star appears just to the left of the galaxy’s bright central bulge but is located between us and the galaxy.”
“Its four diffraction spikes are the result of light bending around the internal supports that hold Hubble’s secondary mirror.”
The image is part of a Hubble survey of 260 satellite galaxies orbiting 22 Milky Way-like host galaxies within about 32 million light-years of Earth.
The astronomers have observed 111 of them so far; the remaining 149 will need one orbit each.
“Low-mass galaxies like the ones in this Hubble observing program provide a way to test the predictions of cosmological models on small scales, which struggle to match observations,” they explained.
“The data Hubble gathers will help us better understand and characterize the properties of low-mass galaxies in Milky Way-like systems, allowing researchers to refine cosmological models.”
